advances: Equality classification for the restricted number of positive bases. Neither an unrestricted sharp lower bound nor an extremizer reduction is used.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
A containing cap at any point of a positive fiber contributes at least the ordinary raw depth on that fiber, by restriction to the base. Thus a largest fiber gives a mark of raw depth at least $\Gamma_d\max_{p\in P}|K_p|$ by 03bc771bddd39a8a. If $|P|<2^n$, or if $|P|=2^n$ and its fiber volumes are unequal, this is strictly greater than $\Gamma_dM/2^n$. Therefore equality forces exactly $2^n$ equal volumes. In that case if a positive fiber is not a simplex, its ordinary maximum is strictly greater than $\Gamma_d|K_p|$ by the same fact. If a positive base is nonvertex, the strict anchored-depth theorem gives a mark of mixed depth strictly greater than its ordinary maximum, which is at least $\Gamma_d|K_p|$. Either strict inequality precludes equality.

At a vertex of the finite positive base hull, some real linear functional strictly exposes it among the positive bases. Use the exposing tilt of 2acc8bc803acf1c0. If $\ell$ strictly exposes $w$ among the positive bases, extend any own through-cap $u\cdot(x-y)\ge0$ by adding $R(\ell(z)-\ell(w))$ to its margin. For sufficiently large finite $R$, boundedness and strict exposure exclude all other positive fibers. This works also when $C$ has deficient ambient rank. Taking infima and using the own-trace lower bound gives pointwise equality. When all four conditions hold, the ordinary simplex maximum from 03bc771bddd39a8a is $\Gamma_d M/2^n$ at each positive fiber. A lattice base in $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ admits a convex representation by positive bases. Convexity puts the corresponding weighted Minkowski sum of their fibers in the fiber at that base. The sum has positive $d$-volume, because at least one positive-weight summand contains a ball. Hence all lattice points in $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ belong to $P$. Any other nonempty fiber has zero volume and its base lies outside that hull, where a pure base closed halfspace containing its base can exclude every positive base by strict separation. Its depth is therefore zero. This proves the converse, the lattice-point claim, and the zero-volume assertion.
statement: Let $n,d\ge1$ and let $C\subset\mathbb R^{n+d}$ be compact and convex. Suppose the set $P$ of its positive $d$-volume integer fibers is nonempty and $|P|\le2^n$. Let $M$ be total mixed $d$-volume and $\Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d$. The maximal normalized closed-halfspace depth on $C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)$ equals $\Gamma_d/2^n$ if and only if $|P|=2^n$, all positive fibers have equal volume, every base in $P$ is a vertex of $\operatorname{conv}(P)$, and every positive fiber is a $d$-simplex. In the equality case the lattice points of $\operatorname{conv}(P)$ are precisely its vertices. Any additional nonempty zero-volume integer fiber has raw depth zero at every point.
title: Sharp depth equality with at most the parity count of positive fibers
